summary.text: 师 is the standardized simplified form of 師. Bronze uses reported for 師 include an official title and troops or an army. Dictionary glosses for 師 also include teacher and master, but the evidence does not establish how these uses are historically connected.

formation.text: The proposed construction of 師 is disputed. One analysis treats 𠂤 as a meaning-bearing element interpreted as a mound and 帀 as a sound element. Other accounts interpret 𠂤 as buttocks or as an abbreviation of 師, while the received Shuowen account explains it as suggesting a multitude. The army-camp-by-a-mound explanation is a proposal, not an established origin.

components.text: One analysis of 師 treats 𠂤 as a meaning-bearing element interpreted as a small mound. Other interpretations identify it as buttocks or as an abbreviation of 師, leaving its original referent and role disputed. This is a proposed component of 師, not a documented internal part of 师.

One analysis identifies 帀 as the sound element in 師; another treats it as meaning-bearing, with the sense “surround.” The proposed sound role remains disputed because the supplied historical comparisons differ.

sound_limitation.text: The modern reading pair and supplied historical comparisons do not independently establish that 帀 functioned as a sound element in 師 or provide a historical sound derivation.

sound.text: The supplied Baxter–Sagart 2014 Middle Chinese forms are 帀 tsop and 師 srij; this comparison does not establish the proposed sound relationship.
The supplied Baxter–Sagart 2014 Old Chinese forms are 帀 *[ts]ˤ[ə]p and 師 *srij; these differ and do not establish the proposed sound relationship.

history.text: The selected seal-script-style image is a modern redraw of the received 師 form, not an excavated inscription. It illustrates a form tradition but does not show a sequence leading to 师 or settle the proposed components’ identities.

師 is the traditional counterpart of standardized simplified 师. The available account does not detail the stages or rationale of simplification. A mnemonic about wielding a knife does not establish the graph’s history.

The reported oracle-bone examples of 師 have unclear uses. Bronze uses are summarized as including an official title and troops or an army; people bearing 師 titles held varied duties, not all directly military. Precise dates and priority among these uses are unresolved.

uncertainties.text: The construction of 師 remains disputed. 𠂤 has been interpreted as a mound, buttocks, or an abbreviation of 師; the proposal that an army camped by a mound is not a demonstrated derivation.
The available evidence does not date teacher and master uses or establish how they relate to the early title and troops-or-army uses.

limitations.text: The oracle-bone examples reported for 師 have unclear uses. Bronze uses are summarized without dated inscription readings, so priority among them is unresolved.
The available glosses do not establish a transition among troops, office, teacher or master, and specialist.

items.caption: A modern redraw of 師 in a seal-script style associated with the received Shuowen tradition. It illustrates that form tradition, not an excavated inscription.
items.alt: A single large black seal-script-style glyph for 師 on a white background.
items.selection_reason: The glyph is legible and illustrates the received form tradition relevant to 師, the traditional counterpart of 师. Its seal-script appearance does not establish the disputed component analysis or a path to the simplified form.
